properties.page_content:
Quantum activation functions
In quantum neural networks programmed on gate-model quantum computers, based on quantum perceptrons instead of variational quantum circuits, the non-linearity of the activation function can be implemented with no need of measuring the output of each perceptron at each layer. The quantum properties loaded within the circuit such as superposition can be preserved by creating the Taylor series of the argument computed by the perceptron itself, with suitable quantum circuits computing the powers up to a wanted approximation degree. Because of the flexibility of such quantum circuits, they can be designed in order to approximate any arbitrary classical activation function. [26]
properties.summary: Quantum neural networks utilize quantum activation functions that allow non-linearity without measuring outputs at each layer. By leveraging quantum properties like superposition, these networks can preserve information through Taylor series approximations. The design of quantum circuits enables the approximation of any classical activation function.

properties.page_content:
Activation function
In artificial  neural  networks, the activation function of  a  node  is  a  function  that  calculates  the output of the node based on its individual inputs and their weights. Nontrivial problems can be solved using only a few nodes if the activation function is nonlinear . [1]
Modern  activation  functions  include  the  logistic  (sigmoid)  function  used  in  the  2012  speech recognition model developed by Hinton et al; [2] the  ReLU used in the 2012 AlexNet computer vision model [3][4] and in the 2015 ResNet model; and the smooth version of the ReLU, the GELU, which was used in the 2018 BERT model. [5]
Comparison of activation functions
Aside from their empirical performance, activation functions also have different mathematical properties:
Nonlinear
When the activation function is non-linear, then a two-layer neural network can be proven to be a universal function approximator. [6]  This is known as the Universal Approximation Theorem. The identity activation function does not satisfy this property. When multiple layers use the identity activation function, the entire network is equivalent to a single-layer model.
Range
When the range of the activation function is finite, gradient-based training methods tend to be more stable, because pattern presentations significantly affect only limited weights. When the range is infinite, training is generally more efficient because pattern presentations significantly affect most of the weights. In the latter case, smaller learning rates are typically necessary.
Continuously differentiable
This property is desirable for enabling gradient-based optimization methods (ReLU is not continuously differentiable and has some issues with gradient-based optimization, but it is still possible). The binary step activation function is not differentiable at 0, and it differentiates to 0 for all other values, so gradient-based methods can make no progress with it. [7]
These properties do not decisively influence performance, nor are they the only mathematical properties that may be useful. For instance, the strictly positive range of the softplus makes it suitable for predicting variances in variational autoencoders.
Mathematical details
The most common activation functions can be divided into three categories: ridge functions, radial functions and fold functions.
An activation function is saturating if . It is nonsaturating if . Non-saturating activation functions, such as ReLU, may be better than saturating activation functions, because they are less likely to suffer from the vanishing gradient problem. [8]
properties.summary: In artificial neural networks, the activation function determines a node's output based on its inputs and weights. Nonlinear activation functions allow for solving complex problems with fewer nodes, as shown by the Universal Approximation Theorem. Modern examples include the logistic function, ReLU, and GELU, each used in various models like speech recognition and computer vision. Activation functions differ in properties such as nonlinearity, range, and differentiability, impacting training stability and efficiency. Non-saturating functions like ReLU are preferred to avoid the vanishing gradient problem. Common activation functions are categorized into ridge, radial, and fold functions.

properties.page_content:
Attention (machine learning)
In  machine learning, attention is  a  method  that  determines  the importance of each component in a sequence relative to the other components  in  that  sequence.  In  natural  language  processing, importance  is  represented  by  "soft"  weights  assigned  to  each word  in  a  sentence.  More  generally,  attention  encodes  vectors called token embeddings across a fixed-width sequence that can range from tens to millions of tokens in size.
Unlike "hard" weights, which are computed during the backwards training pass, "soft" weights exist only in the forward pass  and  therefore  change  with  every  step  of  the  input.  Earlier designs implemented the attention mechanism in a serial
recurrent  neural  network  (RNN)  language  translation  system,  but  a  more  recent  design,  namely  the transformer,  removed  the  slower  sequential  RNN  and  relied  more  heavily  on  the  faster  parallel  attention scheme.
Inspired  by  ideas  about  attention  in  humans,  the  attention  mechanism  was  developed  to  address  the weaknesses  of  using  information  from  the  hidden  layers  of  recurrent  neural  networks.  Recurrent  neural networks  favor  information  contained  in  words  at  the  end  of  a  sentence  and  thus  deemed  more  recent, thereby tending to attenuate the significance and associated predictive weight assigned to information earlier in  the  sentence. Attention  allows  a  token  equal  access  to  any  part  of  a  sentence  directly,  rather  than  only through the previous state.
properties.summary: In machine learning, attention is a method that assesses the importance of each component in a sequence relative to others, using "soft" weights for words in natural language processing. Unlike "hard" weights, which are fixed during training, "soft" weights vary with each input step. Initially implemented in recurrent neural networks (RNNs) for language translation, the transformer model improved efficiency by utilizing a parallel attention scheme. The attention mechanism was inspired by human attention and was designed to overcome RNN limitations, which often prioritize more recent words over earlier ones. This allows tokens to access any part of a sentence directly, enhancing predictive accuracy.

properties.page_content:
War with Sextus Pompey and exile of Lepidus
Before the battles of Philippi, Octavian had sent Salvidienus Rufus to remove  Sextus  Pompey  from  Sicily,  but  after  Rufus's  defeat,  the triumvirs recognized Sextus's Mediterranean command at Brundisium
in 40 BC. [192] When  Sextus resumed his blockade, a starving angry mob in  Rome blamed Octavian and Antony and attacked them in early 39 BC; Antony's forces rescued Octavian  and  dispersed  the  mob. [193] Another temporary  peace  agreement  was  reached  in 39 BC at Misenum. Sextus lifted the blockade on  Italy  once  Octavian  granted  him  Sardinia, Corsica, Sicily, and the Peloponnese and ensured him a future position in the consulship. [194][r]
The  agreement  between  the  triumvirate  and Sextus began to crumble when Octavian divorced Scribonia and married Livia in 38 BC. [200] After Antony refused to relinquish the Peloponnese, Sextus reimposed his blockade, starting food riots at Rome. [201] Sextus's naval commander  Menas  defected, S. C.
A Roman bust of Livia, Augustus's third wife, Musée Saint-Raymond, France
A denarius of Sextus Pompey, minted for his victory over Octavian's fleet. Obverse: the place where he defeated Octavian, Pharus of Messina decorated with a statue of Neptune; before that galley adorned with aquila, sceptre & trident; MAG. PIVS IMP. ITER. Reverse, the monster Scylla, her torso of dogs and fish tails, wielding a rudder as a club. Caption: PRAEF[ECTUS] CLAS[SIS] ET ORAE MARIT[IMAE] EX
handing  over  Corsica  and  Sardinia. [202] However,  after  Octavian's  naval  forces  were  defeated  at Cumae, [203] Octavian  lacked  the  resources  to  confront  Sextus  alone,  so  he  sought  Antony's  help, extending their terms for another five-year period beginning in 37 BC. [204]

document_metadata.section: War with Sextus Pompey and exile of Lepidus

properties.summary: Before the battles of Philippi, Octavian attempted to remove Sextus Pompey from Sicily but faced defeat. In 39 BC, a temporary peace was established, allowing Sextus to lift his blockade in exchange for territories. However, the agreement deteriorated when Octavian divorced Scribonia and married Livia, leading Sextus to reimpose the blockade. This caused food riots in Rome, and Sextus's naval commander defected. After Octavian's defeat at Cumae, he sought Antony's assistance, extending their alliance for another five years.

properties.page_content:
Perusine War, marriage alliances, and Brundisium
Sextus Pompey affirmed his control of Sicily as part of an agreement with the triumvirate in 40 BC, [176] and gained control of Sardinia and Corsica in 39. [177] Both Antony and Octavian sought an alliance with him. [178] Octavian  established  a  temporary  alliance  in  40  BC  when  he  married  Scribonia,  an  aunt  of Sextus's wife. [179] A year later, Scribonia gave birth to Octavian's only surviving child, Julia, on the same day that he divorced her to marry Livia Drusilla. [180] When Livia began her affair with Octavian, she was already married to Tiberius Claudius Nero, had a son Tiberius with Nero, and was pregnant with their second child. She gave birth to her second son, Drusus, several months after her divorce from Nero and marriage to Octavian. [181] Livia later had another child with Octavian, who was born prematurely and did not survive. [182]
While in Egypt, Antony had engaged in an affair with Cleopatra and had fathered three children with her. [183][p] Antony's Gallic provinces fell  into  Octavian's  hands  after  the  death  of Antony's  legate  Quintus Calenus  in  40  BC. [186] Aware  of  his  deteriorating  relationship  with Octavian, Antony  left  Cleopatra;  he  sailed  to  Italy  in  40  BC  with  a large  force  to  oppose  Octavian,  laying  siege  to  Brundisium,  but  the men's  revolting  armies  forced  them  to  reconcile. [187] In  late  40,  the triumvirs divided the empire between Antony in the east, Octavian in the west, and Lepidus in Africa. [188][q] Now in a stronger position due to  the  Parthian  threat  in  Antony's  provinces, [190] Octavian  gave  his sister, Octavia Minor, in marriage to Antony. [191]

document_metadata.section: Perusine War, marriage alliances, and Brundisium

properties.summary: Sextus Pompey secured control of Sicily and formed alliances with Antony and Octavian around 40 BC. Octavian married Scribonia, who bore him a daughter, Julia, before he divorced her for Livia Drusilla. Livia, already married to Tiberius Claudius Nero, had two children with him before marrying Octavian. Meanwhile, Antony had an affair with Cleopatra, resulting in three children. After a conflict with Octavian, Antony attempted to oppose him but was forced to reconcile. By late 40 BC, the triumvirs divided the empire, with Antony in the east and Octavian in the west, and Octavian married his sister to Antony to strengthen their alliance.

properties.page_content:
First conflict with Antony
With opinion in Rome  turning against him and his consulship concluding, Antony illegally  passed  a  law  that  would  assign  him  the province of  Cisalpine  Gaul  in  northern  Italy. [89] Octavian  meanwhile built up a private army in Italy by recruiting Caesarian veterans, [90] and in  early  November entered Rome with this private force to challenge Antony. [91] However, they vacated the city shortly afterwards, [92] due to  some  veterans  choosing  to  quit  once  it  became  clear  they  were involved  in  a  Caesarian  squabble  rather  than  a  revenge  campaign against Caesar's assassins. [93] Nevertheless, on 28 November, Octavian won over two of Antony's legions with the enticing offer of monetary gain. [94] Antony then left Rome for Cisalpine Gaul, [95] which was to be handed  to  him  on  1  January  43  BC. [96] However,  the  province  had earlier  been  assigned  to  the  assassin  Decimus  Junius  Brutus Albinus, who  now  refused  to  yield  to  Antony. [97] Antony  besieged  him  at Mutina. [98] This  provided an opportunity for Octavian, whose private army was at hand. [99]
Flavian-era bust traditionally identified as Mark Antony, Vatican Museums
Cicero defended Octavian against Antony's taunts, [100][h] and had him inducted as a senator on 1 January 43 BC. Octavian was given the power to vote alongside the former consuls, the privilege to stand for election  at  an  earlier  age  than  usual, [102] and imperium pro praetore which  legitimized  his  command.
Bust of Marcus Tullius Cicero, 1st century AD, Capitoline Museums, Rome
Octavian accompanied the consuls to relieve the siege of Mutina. [103] He  assumed  the  fasces  on  7  January, [104] a  date  that  he  would  later commemorate  as  the  beginning  of  his  public  career. [105]   Antony retreated  to  Transalpine  Gaul  after  his  forces  were  defeated  at  the battles  of  Forum  Gallorum  and  Mutina  in  April.  Both  consuls  were killed, however, leaving Octavian in sole command of their armies. [106] These victories  earned  him  his  first  acclamation  as imperator ,  a  title reserved for victorious commanders. [107]
properties.summary: Antony faced opposition in Rome as he illegally passed a law to gain control of Cisalpine Gaul. Octavian built a private army and entered Rome to challenge him but retreated when veterans lost interest. On November 28, Octavian won over two of Antony's legions with monetary incentives. Antony then left for Cisalpine Gaul, which was contested by Decimus Junius Brutus Albinus. Antony besieged Brutus at Mutina, allowing Octavian to act. Cicero defended Octavian, who was inducted as a senator and given significant powers. Octavian joined the consuls to relieve the siege and commemorated January 7 as the start of his public career. After defeating Antony's forces at Forum Gallorum and Mutina, Octavian became the sole commander of the armies and earned the title of imperator.
themes: Victories at Forum Gallorum and Mutina

properties.page_content:
Remodeling of Rome
Augustus  had  the  temples  of  Caesar,  Jupiter  Tonans,  and Apollo Palatinus erected, as well as the Baths of Agrippa and the  Forum  of  Augustus  with  its  Temple  of  Mars  Ultor.  He encouraged  the  establishment  of  the  Theatre  of  Balbus  and Agrippa's construction of the Pantheon, and funded additional projects in the name of others, often relations (e.g. Portico of Octavia, Theatre of Marcellus). [575]   Even his tomb in Rome was built before his death to house members of his family. [576] To  celebrate  his  victory  at  the  Battle  of Actium, the Arch of Augustus was built in 29 BC near the entrance of the Temple of Castor and Pollux, and widened in 19 BC to include a triple-arch  design. [577] He  also  completed  projects left unfinished by Julius Caesar, [578] such as the Curia Julia, the Forum of Caesar, and the Temple of Venus Genetrix. [579] He rebuilt the Basilica Aemilia by 2 BC (previously burned Augustus also provided grand spectacles in Rome. The amphitheater constructed by Statilius Taurus from 34 to 29 BC was the first stone amphitheater built in the city, and opened with gladiator games around the time Octavian staged shows of live combat and the first ever killing of a rhino and hippopotamus for entertainment in Rome. [581] Augustus staged lion hunts in the Circus Maximus, temporarily flooded the Circus Flaminius for slaughtering crocodiles, and held gladiatorial bouts in the Saepta Julia. [582]  In 2 BC he also staged an elaborate mock naval battle, the naumachia Augusti , by creating an artificial lake on the west bank of the Tiber, its waters fed by a newly built aqueduct, the Aqua Alsietina that stretched for over twenty miles. In a lethal performance, the combatants reenacted the 480 BC Battle of Salamis between the Greek city-states led by Athens and the Persian Achaemenid Empire. [583][ap]
properties.summary: Augustus remodeled Rome by erecting significant structures such as temples, baths, and forums, including the Temple of Mars Ultor and the Pantheon. He completed unfinished projects from Julius Caesar, rebuilt the Basilica Aemilia, and celebrated victories with grand spectacles. Notable events included gladiator games, lion hunts, and a mock naval battle in an artificial lake, showcasing his influence on Roman entertainment and architecture.

properties.page_content:
Heir to Caesar
In  44  BC,  Octavius  was  at  Apollonia,  Illyria,  when  Julius Caesar was made Rome's first dictator perpetuo ('dictator in perpetuity') in February, [55] and then assassinated on the Ides of  March  (15  March). [56] Octavius  consulted  with  Caesar's officers in Macedonia before sailing for Italy to ascertain his political fortunes. [57] Caesar had no living legitimate children under Roman law. [58] His  will  made  Octavius  his  main  heir with the condition that he assume the dead dictator's name. [59] After landing near Brundisium in southern Italy, [60] Octavius received  a  copy  of  the  will,  which  bequeathed  him  threequarters  of  Caesar's  estate. [61][f] Against  the  advice  of  his
The Death of Caesar by Vincenzo Camuccini, 1805, Galleria Nazionale d'Arte Moderna, Rome
stepfather  Philippus,  Octavius  accepted  Caesar's  will  on  8  May  44  BC. [64] He  purported  that  Caesar adopted him as his son and assumed the name Gaius Julius Caesar. [65] His stepfather, Cicero, and other contemporaries referred to him as Octavianus . [66]
Octavian could not rely on his limited funds to make a successful entry into politics. [67]  After a warm welcome by Caesar's soldiers at Brundisium, [68] he demanded a portion of the funds allotted by Caesar for his eastern war against the Parthians. [67] This amounted to 700 million sesterces stored at Brundisium, the staging ground in Italy for military operations in the east. [69][g]   Octavian made another bold move when, without official permission, he appropriated the annual tribute from Rome's province of Asia to Italy. [71] He also began to recruit Caesar's veterans and men designated for the Parthian war. [72] On his march to Rome through Italy, Octavian's presence and newly acquired riches won over many, including Caesar's veterans stationed in Campania. [73] By June, he had gathered an army of 3,000 men, paying each a bonus of 500 denarii , [74] which was more than twice a soldier's annual pay. [75]
properties.summary: In 44 BC, Octavius was in Illyria when Julius Caesar was declared dictator perpetuo and subsequently assassinated. He consulted with Caesar's officers before returning to Italy, where he learned he was named Caesar's main heir in the will, inheriting three-quarters of his estate. Despite his stepfather's advice, Octavius accepted the will and adopted the name Gaius Julius Caesar. Lacking funds for a political career, he demanded a portion of Caesar's war funds and appropriated tribute from Asia. He began recruiting Caesar's veterans and, by June, had amassed an army of 3,000 men, offering them significant bonuses.

properties.page_content:
Written works
Augustus  composed  an  account  of  his  achievements,  the Res  Gestae Divi Augusti , to be inscribed in bronze in front of his mausoleum. [527] Copies  of  the  text  were  inscribed  throughout  the  empire  upon  his death. [528] The Latin inscriptions, along with Greek translations, were inscribed  on  many  public  edifices,  and  historian  Theodor  Mommsen called them  the  "queen  of  inscriptions". [529] The Res  Gestae is Augustus's  only  surviving  major  work,  though  he  is  also  known  to have composed poems entitled "Sicilia", "Epiphanus", and "Ajax", an autobiography  of  13  books,  a  philosophical  treatise,  and  a  written rebuttal to Brutus's Eulogy of Cato . [530] Augustus's private letters also reveal facts about his personal life. [531] The  poet  Martial  preserved a sexually crude poem allegedly written by Octavian during the Perusine War, which pokes fun at Mark Antony, his wife Fulvia, and his mistress Glaphyra. [532] Pliny  the  Elder  suggested  that Augustus  displayed  and finished  Agrippa's world  map  publicly  exhibited  in the Porticus
The Roman cameo of Augustus at the center of the medieval Cross of Lothair, housed in the Aachen Cathedral Treasury
Vipsania. [533] This map would later form the basis of various medieval world maps. [534]
In  his Res  Gestae ,  Augustus  defined  the  relative  peace  established  by  his  reign  as  a  peace  "born  of victories" ( parta victoriis pax ) in the civil wars, and Augustan artwork incorporates this theme. [535] This peace  ensured  Romans  and  subjugated  peoples  within  their  Empire  upheld  a  cohesive  social  pact:  the latter would relinquish their sovereignty and pay taxes in exchange for the preservation of their customs and the protection of Rome. [536] By boasting of his many conquests, the Res Gestae emphasizes the same code of honor found in Republican funerary inscriptions such as those of the Scipios, a key element in elevating the political reputation of Roman families. [537]
properties.summary: Augustus authored the Res Gestae Divi Augusti, a record of his achievements inscribed in bronze across the empire after his death. This work, along with Latin and Greek translations, was praised by historian Theodor Mommsen as the 'queen of inscriptions.' Although the Res Gestae is his only major surviving work, Augustus also wrote poems, an autobiography, a philosophical treatise, and letters revealing personal insights. The poet Martial preserved a crude poem by Octavian that humorously targeted Mark Antony and others. Augustus's Res Gestae highlights the peace established during his reign as a 'peace born of victories,' promoting a social pact where subjugated peoples exchanged sovereignty for protection and customs preservation. The work also emphasizes Augustus's conquests, enhancing the political reputation of Roman families.

properties.page_content:
Modern perspectives
Views on Augustus varied during the early modern period. The AngloIrish  writer  Jonathan  Swift  criticized Augustus  for  installing  tyranny over  Rome,  likening  the  virtues  of  the  previous  Roman  Republic  to those  of  Great  Britain's  constitutional  monarchy. [623] French  political philosopher  Montesquieu  remarked  that  Augustus  was  a  coward  in battle, [624] and  English  playwright  William  Shakespeare  portrayed 'Caesar'  as  such  in  his  1607  play Antony  &  Cleopatra . [625] Scottish scholar  Thomas  Blackwell  deemed  Augustus  a  bloodthirsty  usurper and tyrant, [624] views that were shared by Montesquieu and Voltaire. [626] During the 19th century Augustus was widely considered a reformer who brought peace and prosperity after the chaos caused by a  failed  Republic, [627] though  Napoleon  Bonaparte  emulated  Julius Caesar as a role model and was slightly dismissive of Augustus. [628]
Attitudes about Augustus shifted once again during the 20th century, [629] as  scholarship  during  the  upheavals  of  fascism  in  the 1930s  and  1940s  generally  held  negative  views  about  Augustus's seizure of power. [630] In 1937-1938, Benito Mussolini held  an 'Augustan exhibition' in Rome to celebrate the bimillenary of the birth of Augustus, an event which influenced architectural trends of Fascist Italy. [631] Mussolini also styled himself as Il Duce after dux Augustus. [632] Ronald Syme expressed apprehension about Mussolini's espousal  of Augustus. [633] He  sparked  debate  by  publishing  the  then
The Chiaramonti Caesar bust, a posthumous portrait of Julius Caesar in marble, 44-30 BC, Museo Pio-Clementino, Vatican Museums
controversial The Roman Revolution (1939)  at  the  onset  of  the  Second World War,  acknowledging the political climate that impacted his research. [634] He rejected fascist appropriations of ancient Rome while examining  deceptive  political  terminology  employed  by  totalitarian  regimes. [635] Subsequently  more peaceful times have led to a greater focus on the art and literature produced in the Augustan age. [636] In 2014  the  historian  Adrian  Goldsworthy  stressed  that,  in  modern  terms,  Augustus  was  essentially  a military  dictator, [637] but  argued  that  Augustus  was  no  more  ruthless  than  "other  warlords",  and  that comparing him to Mussolini or other modern dictators is anachronistic and inaccurate. [638]
properties.summary: Views on Augustus have evolved over time, with early modern critics like Jonathan Swift and Montesquieu portraying him negatively as a tyrant and coward. In contrast, the 19th century saw him viewed as a reformer who restored peace after the Republic's chaos. The 20th century brought renewed criticism, particularly during the rise of fascism, with figures like Mussolini appropriating Augustus's image for political purposes. Ronald Syme's work in 1939 challenged fascist interpretations of Augustus, emphasizing the need to understand the historical context. More recent scholarship has recognized Augustus as a military dictator, but argues that comparisons to modern dictators are misleading.

properties.page_content:
War and expansion
By AD 13, Augustus's troops had proclaimed him imperator 21 times following  successful  battles. [421] The  fourth  chapter  in  his  publicly released  memoirs  of  achievements  known  as  the Res  Gestae is devoted  to  his  military  victories  and  honors. [422] Augustus  also promoted the ideal of a superior Roman civilization, a sentiment the poet  Virgil  attributed  to  a  legendary  ancestor  of  Augustus. [377] All classes at Rome apparently sought expansionism, and this impulse is accorded divine sanction in Virgil's Aeneid , in which Jupiter promises Rome imperium sine fine ('sovereignty without end'). [423][aj]
By  the  end  of  Augustus's  reign,  his  armies  had  conquered  northern Hispania (modern Spain and Portugal) and the Alpine regions of Raetia and Noricum (modern Switzerland, Bavaria, Austria, Slovenia), Illyricum  and  Pannonia  (modern  Albania,  Croatia,  Hungary,  Serbia, etc.), and had extended the borders of Africa Proconsularis to the east and  south. [425] Judea  was  added  to  the  province  of  Syria  when Augustus  deposed  the  client  king  Herod  Archelaus. [426] After  the Senate assigned Syria to Augustus in 27 BC, it was governed first by legates under Agrippa [427] and then by an equestrian high prefect. [425] In AD 6 Augustus also appointed an equestrian governor in Sardinia after pirate raids necessitated the presence of troops stationed there. [428]
In 25 BC the Romans made Galatia (part of modern Turkey) a province without any military effort after the murder of its king, Amyntas, [429] while  in  19  BC  Agrippa  incorporated  Asturias  and  Cantabria  in
Bust of Augustus wearing the Civic Crown, at Glyptothek, Munich
A fragment of an equestrian statue of Augustus, 1st century BC, National Archaeological Museum, Athens
properties.summary: By AD 13, Augustus had been proclaimed imperator 21 times due to his military successes, which he detailed in his memoirs, the Res Gestae. He promoted the idea of a superior Roman civilization, supported by Virgil's Aeneid, which suggested divine approval for expansionism. By the end of his reign, Augustus's armies had conquered regions including northern Hispania, the Alpine areas, Illyricum, and Pannonia, and expanded Africa Proconsularis. Judea was added to Syria after the deposition of Herod Archelaus. Augustus governed Syria through legates and later appointed an equestrian governor in Sardinia due to pirate threats. In 25 BC, Galatia became a province without military action following the murder of its king, and in 19 BC, Agrippa incorporated Asturias and Cantabria.

properties.page_content:
Early life
Julius  Caesar  had  formed  an  informal  alliance with Pompey and Crassus in 60 BC, [43] but by 49  BC  it  had  fallen  apart  and  Pompey  and Caesar were fighting a protracted civil war. [44] In 47 BC, after Octavius donned the toga virilis and became an adult citizen, [45] Caesar had him elected  as  pontiff,  replacing  the  slain  Lucius Ahenobarbus. [46] The following year, Octavius presided over the Greek games commemorating the opening of Caesar's Temple of  Venus Genetrix. [47] He  wished  to  join  Caesar's  staff for  the  African  campaign  but  gave  way  when his mother Atia protested over his poor health. [48] Caesar allowed Octavius to proceed next to his chariot during his triumph celebrating the campaign and awarded Octavius with military decorations as if he had been  present. [49] In  45  BC  Octavius  traveled  to  Hispania  to  join  Caesar's  Spanish  campaign  against Pompey the Younger. [50] On 13 September 45 BC Caesar deposited a new will with the Vestal Virgins naming Octavius as his principal heir. [51][e]

properties.summary: Julius Caesar formed an alliance with Pompey and Crassus in 60 BC, but by 49 BC, they were in a civil war. In 47 BC, Caesar had Octavius elected as pontiff after he became an adult citizen. Octavius presided over the Greek games for Caesar's Temple of Venus Genetrix and wished to join Caesar's African campaign but was held back by his mother. Caesar honored Octavius during his triumph and awarded him military decorations. In 45 BC, Octavius joined Caesar's Spanish campaign against Pompey the Younger. On September 13, 45 BC, Caesar named Octavius as his principal heir in a new will.

properties.page_content:
Dimensionality reduction
Dimensionality reduction was one of the first deep learning applications. [2]
For Hinton's 2006 study, [10] he pretrained a multi-layer autoencoder with a stack of RBMs and then used their  weights  to  initialize  a  deep  autoencoder  with  gradually  smaller  hidden  layers  until  hitting  a bottleneck of 30 neurons. The resulting 30 dimensions of the code yielded a smaller reconstruction error compared  to  the  first  30  components  of  a  principal  component  analysis  (PCA),  and  learned  a representation that was qualitatively easier to interpret, clearly separating data clusters. [2][10]
Reducing dimensions can improve performance on tasks such as classification. [2] Indeed, the hallmark of dimensionality reduction is to place semantically related examples near each other. [39]
Principal component analysis
If  linear  activations  are  used,  or  only  a  single  sigmoid  hidden  layer,  then  the  optimal  solution  to  an autoencoder  is  strongly  related  to  principal  component  analysis  (PCA). [30][40] The  weights  of  an autoencoder with a single hidden layer of size (where is less than the size of the input) span the same vector  subspace  as  the  one  spanned  by  the  first principal components, and the output of the autoencoder is an orthogonal  projection  onto  this  subspace.  The  autoencoder weights  are  not  equal  to  the  principal  components,  and  are generally  not  orthogonal,  yet  the  principal  components  may be recovered from them using the singular value decomposition. [41]
However, the potential of autoencoders resides in their nonlinearity, allowing the model to learn more powerful generalizations compared to PCA, and to reconstruct the input with significantly lower information loss. [10]
Information retrieval
Information retrieval benefits particularly from dimensionality  reduction  in  that  search  can  become  more efficient in certain kinds of low dimensional spaces. Autoencoders  were  indeed  applied to semantic hashing, proposed  by  Salakhutdinov  and  Hinton  in 2007. [39]   By training  the  algorithm  to  produce  a  low-dimensional  binary code,  all  database  entries  could  be  stored  in  a  hash  table mapping binary code vectors to entries. This table would then support information retrieval by returning all entries with the same binary code as the query, or slightly less similar entries by flipping some bits from the query encoding.
properties.summary: Dimensionality reduction, a key application in deep learning, was demonstrated in Hinton's 2006 study using a multi-layer autoencoder. This method achieved a smaller reconstruction error compared to principal component analysis (PCA) by reducing data to 30 dimensions, enhancing interpretability and clustering. It improves classification performance by placing semantically related examples closer together. When using linear activations, autoencoders relate closely to PCA, but their nonlinearity allows for more powerful generalizations and lower information loss. Dimensionality reduction also aids information retrieval, making searches more efficient in low-dimensional spaces. Autoencoders have been applied to semantic hashing, enabling efficient database storage and retrieval through low-dimensional binary codes.

This is a desired property, as it means small variation in the message leads to small, perhaps even zero, variation in its code, like how two pictures may look the same even if they are not exactly the same. The CAE can be understood as an infinitesimal limit of DAE: in the limit of small Gaussian input noise, DAEs  make  the  reconstruction  function  resist  small  but  finite-sized  input  perturbations,  while  CAEs make  the  extracted  features  resist  infinitesimal  input  perturbations.  However,  while  DAEs  encourage robustness of reconstruction, CAEs  encourage  robustness  of  representation.  Additionally,  DAEs' robustness is obtained stochastically, by having various corrupted versions of a training point aim for an identical reconstruction. In contrast, CAEs' robustness to small perturbations is obtained analytically by penalizing  the  Frobenius  norm  of  the  encoder  Jacobian, ,  evaluated  at  the  training samples [18] .
Minimum description length autoencoder (MDL-AE)
A minimum  description  length  autoencoder (MDL-AE)  is  an  advanced  variation  of  the  traditional autoencoder, which leverages principles from information theory, specifically the Minimum Description Length  (MDL)  principle.  The  MDL  principle  posits  that  the  best  model  for  a  dataset  is  the  one  that provides the shortest combined encoding of the model and the data. In the context of autoencoders, this principle is applied to ensure that the learned representation is not only compact but also interpretable and efficient for reconstruction. The MDL-AE seeks to minimize the total description length of the data, which includes the size of the latent representation (code length) and the error in reconstructing the original data. The objective can be expressed as ,  where represents the length of the compressed latent representation and denotes the reconstruction error. [19]

It contrasts the capabilities of Denoising Autoencoders (DAEs) and Contractive Autoencoders (CAEs) in terms of robustness, with DAEs focusing on reconstruction and CAEs on representation. The Minimum Description Length Autoencoder (MDL-AE) is introduced as an advanced autoencoder that applies the Minimum Description Length principle from information theory to create compact and interpretable representations. The MDL-AE aims to minimize the total description length, which includes both the latent representation size and reconstruction error.

properties.page_content:
Backpropagation
In machine learning, backpropagation is a gradient computation method commonly used for training a neural network in computing parameter updates.
It is an efficient application of the chain rule to neural networks. Backpropagation efficiently computes the gradient of the loss with respect to the network weights for a single input-output example. It does this by propagating derivatives backward, one layer at a time, from the output layer to the input layer, thereby avoiding redundant chain-rule calculations.
Strictly  speaking,  the  term backpropagation refers  only  to  an  algorithm  for  efficiently  computing  the gradient, not how the gradient is used, but the term is often used loosely to refer to the entire learning algorithm. This includes changing model parameters in the negative direction of the gradient, such as by stochastic gradient descent, or as an intermediate step in a more complicated optimizer, such as Adaptive Moment Estimation. [1]
Backpropagation had multiple discoveries and partial discoveries, with a tangled history and terminology (see § History). Some other names for the technique include "reverse mode of automatic differentiation" or "reverse accumulation". [2]
properties.summary: Backpropagation is a gradient computation method used in machine learning for training neural networks by efficiently computing parameter updates. It applies the chain rule to calculate the gradient of the loss with respect to network weights for a single input-output example, propagating derivatives backward from the output to the input layer. While the term specifically refers to the gradient computation algorithm, it is often used to describe the entire learning process, including parameter updates via methods like stochastic gradient descent. The technique has a complex history with various names, such as 'reverse mode of automatic differentiation' or 'reverse accumulation.'

properties.page_content:
Early successes
Contributing to the acceptance were several applications in training neural networks via backpropagation, sometimes achieving popularity outside the research circles. In 1987, NETtalk learned to convert English text into pronunciation. Sejnowski tried training it with both backpropagation and Boltzmann machine, but found the backpropagation significantly faster, so he used it for the final NETtalk. [32]: 324 The NETtalk program became a popular success, appearing on the Today show. [42] In 1989, Dean A. Pomerleau published ALVINN, a neural network trained to drive autonomously using backpropagation. [43] The LeNet was published in 1989 to recognize handwritten zip codes. In 1992, TD-Gammon achieved top human level play in backgammon. It was a reinforcement learning agent with a neural network with two layers, trained by backpropagation. [44] In 1993, Eric Wan won an international pattern recognition contest through backpropagation. [45][46]
After backpropagation
During the 2000s it fell out of favour, but returned in the 2010s, benefiting from cheap, powerful GPUbased  computing  systems.  This  has  been  especially  so  in  speech  recognition,  machine  vision,  natural language processing, and language structure learning research (in  which  it  has  been  used  to  explain  a variety of phenomena related to first [47] and second language learning. [48] ) [49] Error  backpropagation  has  been  suggested  to  explain  human  brain  event-related  potential  (ERP) components like the N400 and P600. [50] In 2023, a backpropagation algorithm was implemented on a photonic processor by a team at Stanford University. [51]
properties.summary: Early applications of backpropagation in neural networks led to notable successes, such as NETtalk, which converted English text to pronunciation, and ALVINN, an autonomous driving neural network. The LeNet model recognized handwritten zip codes, while TD-Gammon achieved top-level play in backgammon. Although backpropagation fell out of favor in the 2000s, it regained popularity in the 2010s due to advancements in GPU computing, impacting fields like speech recognition and natural language processing. Research has suggested that backpropagation may explain certain human brain activities, and in 2023, a backpropagation algorithm was successfully implemented on a photonic processor at Stanford University.

properties.page_content:
Internal covariate shift
Each layer in a neural network has inputs that follow a specific distribution, which shifts during training due to two main factors: the random starting values of the network's settings (parameter initialization) and the natural variation in the input data. This shifting pattern affecting the inputs to the network's inner layers is called internal covariate shift . While a strict definition is not fully agreed upon, experiments show that it involves changes in the means and variances of these inputs during training. Batch  normalization  was  first  developed  to  address  internal  covariate  shift. [1] During  training,  as  the parameters of preceding layers adjust, the distribution of inputs to the current layer changes accordingly, such  that  the  current  layer  needs  to  constantly  readjust  to  new  distributions.  This  issue  is  particularly severe  in  deep  networks,  because  small  changes  in  shallower  hidden  layers  will  be  amplified  as  they propagate within the network, resulting in significant shift in deeper hidden layers. Batch normalization was proposed to reduced these unwanted shifts to speed up training and produce more reliable models. Beyond  possibly tackling internal covariate shift, batch normalization offers several additional advantages. It allows the network to use a higher learning rate-a setting that controls how quickly the network learns-without causing problems like vanishing or exploding gradients, where updates become too small or too large. It also appears to have a regularizing effect, improving the network's ability to generalize to new data, reducing the need for dropout, a technique used to prevent overfitting (when a model  learns  the  training  data  too  well  and  fails  on  new  data).  Additionally,  networks  using  batch normalization  are  less  sensitive  to  the  choice  of  starting  settings  or  learning  rates,  making  them  more
robust and adaptable.
properties.summary: Internal covariate shift occurs in neural networks when the distribution of inputs to layers changes during training due to parameter initialization and input data variation. This shift can affect the means and variances of inputs, particularly in deep networks where changes in earlier layers are amplified. Batch normalization was developed to address this issue by stabilizing the input distributions, allowing for faster training and more reliable models. It enables the use of higher learning rates without the risk of vanishing or exploding gradients. Additionally, batch normalization improves generalization, reducing the need for dropout, and makes networks more robust to initial settings and learning rates.

properties.page_content:
Inference
During  the  training  stage,  the  normalization  steps  depend  on  the  mini-batches  to  ensure  efficient  and reliable training. However, in the inference stage, this dependence is not useful any more. Instead, the normalization  step  in  this  stage  is  computed  with  the  population  statistics  such  that  the  output  could depend on the input in a deterministic manner. The population statistics thus is a complete representation of the mini-batches.

where is  passed  on  to  next  layers  instead  of .  Since  the  parameters  are  fixed  in  this transformation,  the  batch  normalization  procedure  is  essentially  applying  a  linear  transform  to  the activation function.
Although batch normalization has become popular due to its strong empirical performance, the working mechanism of the method is not yet well-understood. The explanation made in the original paper [1]  was that batch norm works by reducing internal covariate shift, but this has been challenged by more recent work. One experiment [5] trained a VGG-16 network [6] under 3 different training regimes: standard (no batch  norm),  batch  norm,  and  batch  norm  with  noise  added  to  each  layer  during  training.  In  the  third model, the noise has non-zero mean and non-unit variance, i.e. it explicitly  introduces  covariate  shift. Despite this, it showed similar accuracy to the second model, and both performed better than the first, suggesting that covariate shift is not the reason that batch norm improves performance.
Using batch normalization causes the items in a batch to no longer be iid, which can lead to difficulties in training due to lower quality gradient estimation. [7]
properties.summary: During training, normalization relies on mini-batches for efficiency, but during inference, it uses population statistics for deterministic output. The population mean and variance represent the mini-batches, and the batch normalization transform applies a linear transformation to the activation function. Despite its popularity, the mechanism of batch normalization is not fully understood. Initial explanations suggested it reduces internal covariate shift, but recent experiments challenge this view. One study showed that adding noise during training did not hinder performance, indicating covariate shift may not be the reason for batch norm's effectiveness. Additionally, batch normalization can disrupt the independence of items in a batch, complicating training due to poorer gradient estimation.

properties.page_content:
Date
Ancient  historians  rarely  provide  the  precise  dates  for  the events they describe. For example, Livy provides no explicit dates for  any  of  the  battles  of  the  Second  Punic  War. Macrobius, citing the Roman  annalist Quintus  Claudius Quadrigarius, states the battle was fought ante diem iiii nones Sextilis , or 2 August. [32]
The months of the pre-Julian Roman calendar are known not to correspond to its namesake Julian day. For example, Livy records a lunar eclipse in 168 BC  as  occurring on  4 September, when astronomical calculations show it happened on Julian day 21 June of that year. [33] This discrepancy arose from the failure of the pontifices to properly perform
A modern monument near the site of the Battle of Cannae
intercalations, either by accident or for political advantage. A review of the evidence led P. S. Derow to identify  the  equivalent  Julian  date  as  1  July  216  BC.  Other  authorities  have  suggested  other  Julian dates. [34]
Armies
Figures  for  troops  involved  in  ancient  battles  are  often  unreliable,  and  Cannae  is  no  exception.  They should be treated with caution, especially those for the Carthaginian side. [35]  The Carthaginian army was a combination of warriors from numerous regions, and may have numbered between 40,000 and 50,000. Their infantry comprised an estimated 8,000 Libyans, 5,500 Gaetulian, 16,000 Gauls, mainly Boii and Insubres (8,000 were left at camp the day of battle) and 8,000 of several tribes of Hispania, including Iberians, Celtiberians and Lusitanians. [36]
Hannibal's cavalry also came from diverse backgrounds. He commanded 4,000 Numidian, 2,000 Iberian peninsular,  4,000  Gallic  and  450  Libyan-Phoenician  cavalry.  Hannibal  had  an  auxiliary  skirmisher contingent consisting of 1,000-2,000 Balearic slingers and 6,000 mixed-nationality javelinmen, possibly including Lusitanians among them. [37] The uniting factor for the Carthaginian army was the personal tie each group had with Hannibal. [38][39]
properties.summary: Ancient historians often lack precise dates for events, as seen with Livy's accounts of the Second Punic War. Discrepancies in the Roman calendar, such as a lunar eclipse recorded by Livy, highlight issues with intercalations. The Battle of Cannae's troop figures are also unreliable, with estimates for the Carthaginian army ranging from 40,000 to 50,000, including diverse infantry and cavalry units. Hannibal's forces comprised warriors from various regions, united by their loyalty to him.

properties.page_content:
Roman
Polybius writes that of the Roman and allied infantry, 70,000 were killed, 10,000 captured, and "perhaps" 3,000 survived. He also reports that of the 6,000 Roman and allied cavalry, only 370 survived. [85] Livy wrote, "Forty-five thousand and five hundred foot, two thousand seven hundred horse, there being an equal number of citizens and allies, are said to have been slain." [86] He also reports that 3,000 Roman and  allied  infantry  and  1,500  Roman  and  allied  cavalry  were  taken  prisoner  by  the  Carthaginians. [86] Another 2,000 Roman fugitives were rounded up at the unfortified village of Cannae by Carthaginian cavalry  commanded  by  Carthalo,  7,000  fell  prisoner  in  the  smaller  Roman  camp  and  5,800  in  the larger. [86] Although Livy does not cite his source by name, it is likely to have been Quintus Fabius Pictor, a Roman historian who fought in and wrote about the Second Punic War. It is Pictor whom Livy names when reporting the casualties at the Battle of Trebia. [87] In  addition  to  the  consul  Paullus,  Livy  recorded  that  among  the  dead  were  2  quaestors,  29  of  the  48 military  tribunes,  some  of  consular  rank,  including  the  consul  of  the  previous  year,  Gnaeus  Servilius Geminus, and the former magister equitum , Marcus Minucius Rufus, and 80 "senators or men who had held offices which would have given them the right to be elected to the Senate". [86] Later Roman and Greco-Roman historians largely follow Livy's figures. Appian gave 50,000 killed and "a great many" taken prisoner. [88] Plutarch agreed, "50,000 Romans fell in that battle... 4,000 were taken alive  in  the  field  and  10,000  in  the  camps  of  both  consuls". [2] Quintilian:  "60,000  men  were  slain  by Hannibal at Cannae". [89] Eutropius:  "20  officers  of  consular  and  praetorian  rank,  30  senators,  and  300 others of noble descent, were taken or slain, as well as 40,000-foot-soldiers, and 3,500 horse". [90] Some  modern  historians,  while  rejecting  Polybius's  figure  as  flawed,  are  willing  to  accept
properties.summary: Polybius reports that 70,000 Roman and allied infantry were killed, with 10,000 captured and around 3,000 surviving. Of the 6,000 cavalry, only 370 survived. Livy states that 45,500 foot soldiers and 2,700 horse were slain, with 3,000 infantry and 1,500 cavalry taken prisoner by the Carthaginians. Additionally, 2,000 Roman fugitives were captured at Cannae. Livy likely relied on Quintus Fabius Pictor for his casualty figures. Among the dead were high-ranking officials, including consuls and senators. Later historians like Appian and Plutarch echoed Livy's figures, with estimates of 50,000 killed and many taken prisoner. Quintilian and Eutropius provided varying numbers, indicating the scale of the battle's casualties.

properties.page_content:
Aftermath
Hannibal counting the signet rings of the Roman knights killed during the battle, statue by Sébastien Slodtz, 1704, Louvre pledged his support to Hannibal, initiating the First Macedonian War against Rome. The following year Hannibal secured an alliance with the new king Hieronymus of Syracuse, the only independent king left in Sicily. [101] Livy illustrates the state of Roman morale with two vivid anecdotes. The  first  concerns  Hannibal's  brother  Mago,  who  had  returned  to Carthage with news of the victory. He reported to their senate that in several  engagements  with  the  Romans  Hannibal  had  killed  over 200,000 soldiers and taken 50,000 prisoner; of six commanders met in  battle,  two  consuls  and  a  Master  of  horse  had  been  slain;  and  a number  of  Roman  allies  had  gone  over  to  the  Carthaginians.  Then Mago  concluded  his  report  by  having  a  container  of  golden  rings poured upon the council floor in front of the assembled senators. He explained that each ring belonged to one eques who had been slain in battle  and  had  earned  the  ring  through  exceptional  bravery.  Livy notes  that  one  unnamed  authority  stated  the  volume  of  jewelry amounted to three and one-half measures, only to add "it is generally and more credibly held that there was not more than one measure of them". [102] The  second  concerns  Lucius  Caecilius  Metellus  and  three  other military  tribunes,  who  had  taken  refuge  at  Canusium  with  other Roman  refugees.  Demoralized  at  the  defeat,  they  discussed  the possibility of setting sail  overseas  and  finding  employment  as mercenaries  for  some  foreign  prince. Word  of  this  meeting  reached the  young  Publius  Cornelius  Scipio [103] who,  with  only  a  few followers,  burst  into  the  room  where  the  discussion  was  underway. Holding his naked sword over the heads of the wavering men, Scipio is reported to have cried:
I  swear  with  all  the  passion  in  my  heart  that  I  will  never desert our homeland, or permit any other citizen of Rome to leave  her  in  the  lurch.  If  I  willfully  break  my  oath  may Jupiter,  Greatest  and  Best,  bring  me  to  a  shameful  death, with  my  house,  my  family,  and  all  I  possess!  Swear  the same oath, Caecilius! And the rest of you, swear it too. If anyone refuses, against him this sword is drawn. [104]
properties.summary: After Hannibal's victories, he secured alliances and reported significant Roman losses, claiming over 200,000 soldiers killed and 50,000 captured. His brother Mago presented golden rings from slain Roman knights to the Carthaginian senate as a testament to their bravery. Meanwhile, Roman military tribunes, demoralized by defeat, considered fleeing to become mercenaries. Young Publius Cornelius Scipio intervened, passionately swearing to defend Rome and urging his fellow citizens to do the same, threatening those who would abandon their homeland.

properties.summary: The Battle of Cannae, fought on August 2, 216 BC, during the Second Punic War, resulted in a significant Carthaginian victory. Commanded by Hannibal, the Carthaginian forces defeated a larger Roman army led by Gaius Terentius Varro and Lucius Aemilius Paullus. The battle took place in Cannae, Italy, where the Carthaginians gained a foothold in southern Italy, leading to the defection of some Roman allies. The total strength of the Roman forces was approximately 86,400, while the Carthaginian army numbered around 50,000. The aftermath saw heavy Roman casualties, with 70,000 killed and 10,000 captured.

properties.page_content:
Stars orbiting Sagittarius A*
An M87* image with superimposed lines representing the magnitude and direction of polarisation
The M87* relativistic jet; inset is the black hole shadow
The  Event  Horizon  Telescope  image  of  Sagittarius  A*,  the object  at  the  centre  of  the  Milky  Way,  released  in  2022, provided confirmation that it is indeed a black hole. [45]
The proper motions of stars near the centre of the Milky Way provide  strong  observational  evidence  that  these  stars  are orbiting a supermassive black hole. Astronomers have tracked the  motions  of  over  100  stars  orbiting  an  invisible  object coincident  with  the  radio  source  Sagittarius A*.  One  of  the stars-called S2-completed  a  full  orbit. By  fitting the motions  of  stars  to  Keplerian  orbits,  the  astronomers  were able to infer that the invisible object assumed to be Sagittarius A* must have a mass of 4.3 × 10 6 M ☉ ,  with a radius of less than  0.002  light-years. [213] This  upper  limit  radius  is  larger than the Schwarzschild radius for the estimated mass, so the combination  does  not  prove  Sagittarius  A*  is  a  black  hole.
Stars moving around Sagittarius A*, as seen in 2021
Nevertheless, these observations strongly suggest that the central object is a supermassive black hole as there are no other plausible scenarios for confining so much invisible mass into such a small volume. [39] Additionally, luminosity data from this object implies it must possess an event horizon, a defining feature of  black  holes. [214] By  tracking  the  motion  of  the  centre  it  has  been  shown  that  the  central  object  is motionless at the centre of the galaxy. [215]
properties.summary: The Event Horizon Telescope image of Sagittarius A*, released in 2022, confirmed it as a black hole. Observations of over 100 stars orbiting this invisible object provide strong evidence of its supermassive nature, with one star, S2, completing a full orbit. The inferred mass of Sagittarius A* is 4.3 × 10^6 M ☉, with a radius smaller than 0.002 light-years. Although this radius exceeds the Schwarzschild radius for its mass, the evidence strongly suggests it is a black hole due to the lack of alternative explanations for the concentrated mass. Luminosity data indicates the presence of an event horizon, a characteristic of black holes. Tracking the motion of the center shows that this object remains motionless at the galaxy's center.
