Black  holes  with  the  maximum  possible  combination  of  charge  and  spin satisfying this inequality are called extremal black holes. Adding a low-mass object with a lot of charge or angular momentum to an extremal black hole would create a so-called naked singularity, a singularity outside of a black hole. [62] Because these singularities make the universe inherently unpredictable, many physicists believe they could not exist. [63] The weak cosmic censorship hypothesis, proposed by Penrose,
Radii for shadow and photon sphere relative to the event horizon rules out the formation of such singularities, when they are created through the gravitational collapse of realistic matter. This hypothesis remains an important area of study because has not yet been proven and it relates to many aspects of general relativity and quantum gravity. [64] The  total  mass  of  a  nearby  black  hole  can  be  estimated  by  analysing  the  motion  of  the  stars  or  gas surrounding it. The mass of distant supermassive black holes can be inferred from Doppler broadening of spectral lines emitted by rapidly orbiting gas, a technique called reverberation mapping. [65]
properties.summary: The text discusses black holes, particularly extremal black holes that satisfy a specific inequality involving charge and spin. It mentions that adding a low-mass, highly charged object to an extremal black hole could lead to a naked singularity, which is considered unpredictable and potentially non-existent according to many physicists. The weak cosmic censorship hypothesis, proposed by Penrose, suggests that such singularities cannot form during the gravitational collapse of realistic matter. This hypothesis is significant in the study of general relativity and quantum gravity. Additionally, the mass of nearby black holes can be estimated by observing the motion of surrounding stars or gas, while the mass of distant supermassive black holes can be inferred through techniques like reverberation mapping.

properties.page_content:
Alternatives to black holes
While there is a strong case for supermassive black holes, [250][251] the dividing line between lighter black holes and neutron stars relies on theories of extremely dense matter. Direct observational tests are not available: objects observed to have mass higher than the predictions for neutron stars are assumed to be black holes. Recent evidence from gravitational wave events suggests modifications of these theories may be needed. [80] New exotic phases of matter could allow other kinds of massive objects. [137] Quark stars would be made up of quark matter and supported by quark degeneracy pressure, a form of degeneracy pressure  even  stronger  than  neutron  degeneracy  pressure.  This  would  halt  gravitational  collapse  at  a higher mass than for a neutron star. [252][253] Even stronger stars called electroweak stars would convert quarks in their cores into leptons, providing additional pressure to stop the star from collapsing. [254][255] If, as some extensions of the Standard Model posit, quarks and leptons are made up of the even-smaller fundamental  particles  called  preons,  a  very  compact  star  could  be  supported  by  preon  degeneracy pressure. [256] While none of these hypothetical models can explain all of the observations of stellar black hole  candidates,  a  Q  star  is  the  only  alternative  which  could  significantly  exceed  the  mass  limit  for neutron stars and thus provide an alternative for supermassive black holes. [137]: 12
A  few  theoretical  objects  have  been  conjectured  to  match  observations  of  astronomical  black  hole candidates  identically  or  near-identically,  but  which  function  via  a  different  mechanism. [257] A  dark energy star would convert infalling matter into vacuum energy; this vacuum energy would be much larger than the vacuum energy of outside space, exerting outwards pressure and preventing a singularity from forming. [258][259] A  black  star  would  be  gravitationally  collapsing  slowly  enough  that  quantum  effects would keep it just on the cusp of fully collapsing into a black hole. [260] A gravastar would consist of a very thin shell and a dark-energy interior providing outward pressure to stop the collapse into a black hole or formation of a singularity; It could even have another gravastar inside, called a 'nestar'. [261]
properties.summary: While supermassive black holes are widely accepted, the distinction between lighter black holes and neutron stars is based on theories of dense matter, with recent gravitational wave evidence suggesting these theories may need revision. New exotic matter phases, such as quark stars and electroweak stars, could halt gravitational collapse at higher masses than neutron stars. Hypothetical Q stars might exceed neutron star mass limits, offering alternatives to supermassive black holes. Other theoretical objects like dark energy stars and black stars propose different mechanisms to prevent singularity formation, while gravastars consist of a thin shell with dark-energy interiors to stop collapse.

properties.page_content:
Direct interferometry
The Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) is a global system of radio telescopes capable of directly observing a black hole shadow. [44] The angular resolution of a telescope is based on its aperture and the wavelengths it is observing. Because the angular diameters of Sagittarius A* and Messier 87* in the sky are very small, a single telescope would need to be about the size of the Earth to clearly  distinguish  their  horizons  using  radio  wavelengths.  By combining  data  from  several  different  radio  telescopes  around the  world,  the  Event  Horizon  Telescope  creates  an  effective aperture  the  diameter  size  of  the  Earth.  The  EHT  team  used imaging algorithms to compute the most probable image from the data in its observations of Sagittarius A* and M87*. [209][1]
Gravitational waves
Gravitational-wave interferometry can be used to detect merging black holes and other compact objects. In this method, a laser beam is split, sent down two long arms of a tunnel, then reflected at the far end of the tunnels to reconverge at the intersection of the arms, precisely cancelling each other. However, when a  gravitational  wave  passes,  it  warps  spacetime,  changing  the  relative  lengths  of  the  arms  themselves. Since each laser beam is now travelling a slightly different distance, they do not cancel out and produce a recognisable  signal.  Analysis  of  the  signal  can  give  scientists  information  about  what  caused  the gravitational waves. Since gravitational waves are very weak, gravitational-wave observatories such as LIGO must have arms several kilometres long and carefully control for noise from Earth to be able to detect these gravitational waves. [210] Since the first measurements in 2016, multiple gravitational waves from black holes have been detected and analysed. [91]
A  satellite  based  gravitational  wave  instrument,  LISA,  is  under  construction  with  launch  planned  for approximately 2035. The mission will consist of three spacecraft flying in a triangular formation with 2.5 million km arm lengths to detect low-frequency gravitational waves from sources such as merging supermassive black holes and compact binary systems. [211][212]
properties.summary: The Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) is a network of radio telescopes that can observe black hole shadows by combining data to create an effective aperture the size of Earth. It uses imaging algorithms to analyze observations of Sagittarius A* and M87*. Gravitational-wave interferometry detects merging black holes by measuring changes in the lengths of laser beams caused by passing gravitational waves. This method requires long arms and noise control to identify weak signals. Since 2016, multiple gravitational waves from black holes have been detected. A satellite-based instrument, LISA, is being developed to detect low-frequency gravitational waves from supermassive black holes and binary systems, with a launch planned for around 2035.

properties.page_content:
Formation
Black holes are formed by gravitational collapse of massive stars, either by direct collapse or during a supernova  explosion  in  a  process  called fallback . [168] Black  holes  can  result  from  the  merger  of  two neutron  stars  or  a  neutron  star  and  a  black  hole. [169] Other  more  speculative  mechanisms  include primordial black holes created from density fluctuations in the early universe, the collapse of dark stars, a hypothetical  object  powered  by  annihilation  of  dark  matter,  or  from  hypothetical  self-interacting  dark matter. [170]
properties.summary: Black holes form from the gravitational collapse of massive stars, either directly or during a supernova explosion. They can also result from the merger of two neutron stars or a neutron star with a black hole. Other speculative mechanisms for their formation include primordial black holes from early universe density fluctuations, the collapse of dark stars, or hypothetical objects powered by dark matter annihilation.

properties.page_content:
Charge
Black holes are believed to have an approximately neutral charge. For example, Michal Zajaček, Arman Tursunov, Andreas Eckart, and Silke Britzen found the electric charge of Sagittarius A* to be at least ten orders of magnitude below the theoretical maximum. [71] If a black hole were to become charged, particles with an opposite sign of charge would be pulled in by the extra electromagnetic force, while particles with the same sign of charge would be repelled, neutralising the black hole. This effect operates even more rapidly if the black hole is also spinning. [72] A spinning black hole in a magnetic field creates an electric field which would interact with charged particles. [71] Since black holes have so few measurable intrinsic properties, techniques for measuring charge are of interest to astrophysics even if the values may be very small. [73]
The charge Q for a nonspinning black hole is bounded by
Q ≤√4π∈0GM,
where G is the gravitational constant and M is the black hole's mass. [74]
properties.summary: Black holes are generally considered to have a neutral charge, with studies showing Sagittarius A*'s charge is significantly below theoretical limits. If charged, a black hole would attract oppositely charged particles and repel like charges, potentially neutralizing itself. This effect is enhanced if the black hole is spinning, as it generates an electric field that interacts with charged particles. Measuring the charge of black holes is important in astrophysics, despite their few measurable properties.

properties.page_content:
Other mechanisms
Observations of quasars from less than a billion years after the Big Bang [174][175] has led to investigations of other ways to form black holes. The accretion process to build supermassive black holes has a limiting rate of mass accumulation and a billion years is not enough time to reach quasar status. One suggestion is direct collapse of nearly pure hydrogen gas (low metalicity) clouds characteristic of the young universe, forming a supermassive star which collapses into a black hole. It has been suggested that seed black holes with  typical  masses  of  ~10 5 M ☉ could  have  formed  in  this  way  which  then  could  grow  to  ~10 9 M ☉ . However,  the  very  large  amount  of  gas  required  for  direct  collapse  is  not  typically  stable  against fragmentation which would form multiple stars. Thus another approach suggests massive star formation followed by collisions that seed massive black holes which ultimately merge to create a quasar. [176]: 85 A neutron star in a common envelope with a regular star can accrete sufficient material to collapse to a black hole or two neutron stars can merge. These avenues for the formation of black holes are considered relatively rare. [177]
Primordial black holes and the Big Bang
In  the  early  universe,  fluctuations  of  spacetime  may  have  formed  areas  that  were  denser  than  their surroundings. Rapid early expansion of the universe may have allowed these areas to collapse, forming primordial black holes. [178] Various models predict the creation of primordial black holes ranging from a Planck  mass  (~2.2 × 10 -8 kg)  to  hundreds  of  thousands  of  solar  masses.  Primordial  black  holes  with masses less than 10 12 kg would have evaporated by now due to Hawking radiation. [179] Despite the early universe being extremely dense, it did not re-collapse into a black hole during the Big Bang, since the universe was expanding rapidly and did not have the gravitational differential necessary for black hole formation. Models for the gravitational collapse of objects of relatively constant size, such [180]
as stars, do not necessarily apply in the same way to rapidly expanding space such as the Big Bang.
properties.summary: Investigations into black hole formation suggest that direct collapse of nearly pure hydrogen gas clouds in the young universe could create supermassive stars that collapse into black holes. Seed black holes of around 10^5 solar masses may form this way, but the gas required is often unstable. An alternative theory proposes that massive star formation followed by collisions can lead to the creation of massive black holes. Additionally, primordial black holes may have formed from denser areas in the early universe, with models predicting their mass ranging from Planck mass to hundreds of thousands of solar masses. However, primordial black holes under 10^12 kg would have evaporated due to Hawking radiation. The rapid expansion of the universe during the Big Bang prevented it from collapsing into a black hole.

properties.page_content:
1204-1453: Palaiologos dynasty
Michael desired to restore the empire's glory through a rebuilding programme in Constantinople, clever diplomatic  alliances,  and  expansionist  wars  in  Europe. [163] He  staved  off  the  threatening  Charles  I  of Anjou first by recognising papal primacy and certain Catholic doctrines at the 1274 Second Council of Lyon,  and  then  by  aiding  the  Sicilian  Vespers  against  Charles  in  1282. [164] However,  his  religious concessions were despised by most of the populace, and were repudiated by his successor Andronikos II (r. 1282-1328). [165] He and his grandson Andronikos III (r. 1328-1341) led several campaigns to restore imperial influence, succeeding in Epirus and Thessaly. Their policies also weakened the state, including the  dismissal  of  the  fleet  in  1285,  the  hiring  of  the  mercenary  Catalan  Company,  which  turned  on  the Byzantines in the 1300s, and their civil war between 1320 and 1328. [166] A disastrous civil war between 1341 and 1354 caused long-term economic difficulties, while the Ottoman Turks gradually expanded. [167]
The diminished Byzantine state survived for another century through diplomacy and favourable external developments. [168] The  Ottomans  gradually  subjugated  Anatolia  and  simultaneously  expanded  into Europe from 1354, taking Philippopolis in 1363, Adrianopolis in 1369, and Thessalonica in 1387. [169] Dynastic struggles increasingly depended on Venetian, Genoese, and Ottoman backing. [170] After Manuel II (r. 1391-1425) refused to pay homage to Sultan Bayezid I in 1394, Constantinople was besieged until the  rampaging  warlord  Timur  decisively  defeated  Bayezid  in  1402,  with  the  city  perilously  close  to surrender. [171]
properties.summary: The Palaiologos dynasty aimed to restore the Byzantine Empire's glory through rebuilding, diplomacy, and wars in Europe. Michael, the emperor, initially recognized papal primacy to fend off Charles I of Anjou but faced backlash from the populace. His successors, Andronikos II and Andronikos III, attempted to restore imperial influence but weakened the state through poor policies and civil wars. A significant civil war from 1341 to 1354 led to economic difficulties as the Ottoman Turks expanded into Byzantine territories. Despite these challenges, the Byzantine state survived for another century through diplomacy and external developments, while dynastic struggles increasingly relied on foreign support. The Ottomans gradually conquered Anatolia and Europe, culminating in the siege of Constantinople after Manuel II's refusal to pay homage to Sultan Bayezid I.

properties.page_content:
Byzantine Empire
The Byzantine  Empire ,  also  known  as  the Eastern Roman Empire ,  was  the  continuation  of  the  Roman Empire centred on Constantinople during late antiquity and the Middle Ages. Having survived the fall of the Western  Roman  Empire  in  the  5th  century  AD,  it endured until the fall of Constantinople to the Ottoman Empire  in  1453.  The  term  'Byzantine  Empire'  was coined only after its demise; its citizens used the term 'Roman Empire' and called themselves 'Romans'. [a]
During  the  early  centuries  of  the  Roman  Empire,  the western provinces were Latinised, but the eastern parts kept their Hellenistic culture. Constantine I (r. 324-337) legalised Christianity and moved  the capital  to  Constantinople.  Theodosius  I  (r. 379-395) made Christianity the state religion and Greek gradually  replaced  Latin  for  official  use.  The  empire adopted a defensive strategy and, throughout its remaining  history, experienced  recurring cycles of decline and recovery.
The Byzantine Empire reached its greatest extent under the reign of Justinian I (r. 527-565),  who  briefly reconquered much of Italy and the western Mediterranean coast. A plague began around 541, and a  prolonged  warfare  with  Persia  placed  fiscal  and military strain  on  the  empire,  contributing  to  political and strategic  challenges  in  the  decades  that  followed. In  the  630s  and  640s  the  Arab  conquests  defeated Byzantine field armies in Syria and Egypt, resulting in the permanent loss of those provinces to the Rashidun Caliphate.  In  698,  Africa  was  lost  to  the  Umayyad Caliphate, but the empire stabilised under the Isaurian dynasty. It expanded once more under the Macedonian dynasty, experiencing a two-century-long renaissance. Thereafter,  periods  of  civil  war  and  Seljuk  incursion resulted in the loss of most of Asia Minor. The empire recovered during the Komnenian restoration, and
properties.summary: The Byzantine Empire, also known as the Eastern Roman Empire, was the continuation of the Roman Empire centered on Constantinople, surviving until its fall in 1453. Its citizens referred to themselves as 'Romans' and used the term 'Roman Empire.' The empire maintained its Hellenistic culture while adopting Christianity as the state religion under Theodosius I. It reached its peak under Justinian I, who reconquered parts of Italy and the Mediterranean. However, it faced challenges from plagues, wars with Persia, and Arab conquests, leading to significant territorial losses. Despite periods of decline, the empire experienced a renaissance under the Macedonian dynasty before suffering further losses due to civil wars and incursions.
themes: Fall of the Western Roman Empire

properties.page_content:
718-867: Isaurian, Nikephorian, and Amorian dynasties
Stability was somewhat restored during the reign of Theophilos (r. 829-842). He capitalised on economic growth  to  complete  construction  programmes,  including  rebuilding  the  sea  walls  of  Constantinople, overhaul provincial governance, and wage inconclusive campaigns against the Abbasids. [108] After  his death, his empress Theodora, ruling on behalf of her son Michael III, permanently restored the veneration of  icons; [109] the  empire  prospered  under  their  sometimes-fraught  rule.  Michael  was  posthumously vilified by historians loyal to the dynasty of his successor Basil I, who had him assassinated in 867 and later benefited from successes begun under his predecessor. [110]
properties.summary: During Theophilos' reign (829-842), stability returned as he focused on economic growth and infrastructure, including rebuilding Constantinople's sea walls. After his death, Empress Theodora restored icon veneration while ruling for her son Michael III. Their rule saw prosperity, but Michael III was later vilified by historians loyal to his successor Basil I, who had him assassinated in 867.

properties.page_content:
Economy
The fall of Constantinople during the Fourth Crusade in 1204 destroyed centuries of its wealth. [276] Large landholdings were confiscated, and the empire fragmented into smaller rump states ruled by competing factions,  making  governance  inefficient  and  increasing  the  costs  of  doing  business. [277] The  state gradually lost control over trade practices, price regulations, the outflow of precious metals, and possibly even the minting of coins. [278] Italian merchants further dominated trade as the events of 1204 opened the Black Sea to  Western merchants, permanently altering the empire's fortunes. [279] Farmers  and manufacturers increasingly produced goods for local use and were affected by the insecurity of constant warfare. [280] Despite these challenges, the empire's mixed economy (characterised by state interventions, public works, and market liberalisation) [281] remained a model of medieval economic adaptability, even as it deteriorated under external pressures. [282]
Art and architecture
Subjects in Byzantine art were primarily Christian and typically non-naturalistic in their representation. [285] Emerging  from  both  the  earliest  Christian  and  Late  Antique  art, [286] many  early examples  were  lost  amid  the  Roman  Persecutions;  the  fragmented  mosaics  of  the  3rd-century  DuraEuropos church are a unique exception. [287] Such Byzantine mosaics, known for their gold ground style, became a hallmark of the empire, displaying both secular and sacred themes in diverse places, including churches (Basilica of San Vitale), the circus (Hippodrome of Constantinople), and the Great Palace of Constantinople. [288] The early 6th-century reign of Justinian I saw systemic developments: religious art came to dominate, and once-popular public marble and bronze monumental sculpture fell out of favor due to  pagan  associations. [289] Justinian  commissioned  the  monumental  Hagia  Sophia  church,  and  its influential  elements  became  architectural  hallmarks  for  the  empire:  the  immense  size,  large  dome, innovative use of pendentives and highly decorative interior were imitated as far north as the Cathedral of Saint Sophia in Novgorod and the Saint Sophia Cathedral in Kiev. [290] The Hagia Sophia's creators, the engineer-architects  Isidore  of  Miletus  and  Anthemius  of  Tralles,  are  uniquely  esteemed; [291] most Byzantine artists were unrecorded and typically deemed to have little importance. [292] Smaller-scale  art  flourished  throughout  the  entire  Byzantine  period:  costly  ivory  carvings-often  as
properties.summary: The fall of Constantinople in 1204 led to the fragmentation of the empire, loss of trade control, and increased business costs. Italian merchants gained dominance in trade, altering the empire's economic landscape. Despite challenges, the Byzantine economy showcased adaptability through state interventions and market liberalization. Byzantine art was primarily Christian and non-naturalistic, with mosaics becoming a hallmark of the empire. The reign of Justinian I saw a shift towards religious art, with the Hagia Sophia commissioned as a monumental architectural achievement. Its innovative design influenced future structures across the region, while smaller-scale art thrived throughout the Byzantine period.

properties.page_content:
Military evolution
In  the  late  6th  century,  following  Justinian  I's  wars,  seven  mobile  field  armies  called comitatenses , numbering around 150,000 troops, were deployed around the empire; they remained the finest armies in Europe. [207] They were aided by twenty-five frontier garrisons of approximately 195,000 lower-quality limitanei troops. [208] Additional troops included subsidised allied forces and imperial guard units like the
[209]
Shield insignia of regiments under the command of the Magister Militum Praesentalis II of the East Roman army c. 395 AD. Page from the Notitia Dignitatum Scholae  Palatinae . Naval  forces  were  limited:  flotillas  were based at key locations, while 30,000 oarsmen were assembled to row 500, mostly requisitioned, transports to support the Vandalic War in Africa in 533. [210] The losses suffered in the 7th-century  Arab conquests led to fundamental changes. [211] The field armies were withdrawn into the core Anatolian territories  and  assigned  to  settle  in  specific  districts, which  became  known  as themata and  eventually  replaced  the  old provinces. [212] The  thematic  armies,  supported  by  the  proceeds  of their  districts,  came  to  resemble  a  provincial  militia  with  a  small professional core, aided by foreign mercenaries and imperial regiments at Constantinople. [213] To  defend  against  its  new  Muslim enemy, the navy was similarly reorganised into several provincialised fleets. [214] It became the dominant power in the eastern Mediterranean,  with  dromons  equipped  with  Greek  fire  proving crucial on several occasions. [215] As  the  8th-century  empire  stabilised,  the  thematic  militias  proved rebellious and only suitable for defensive operations. [216]
properties.summary: In the late 6th century, the Byzantine Empire deployed seven mobile field armies, known as comitatenses, totaling around 150,000 troops, supported by 195,000 limitanei troops and allied forces. Naval forces were limited, with 30,000 oarsmen used for transports during the Vandalic War. The Arab conquests in the 7th century led to significant military changes, with field armies being withdrawn to Anatolia and organized into thematic districts. These thematic armies resembled provincial militias, supported by local resources and foreign mercenaries. The navy was reorganized into provincial fleets to counter Muslim threats, becoming a dominant force in the eastern Mediterranean. By the 8th century, the thematic militias were primarily defensive and often rebellious.

properties.page_content:
Pre-518: Constantinian, Theodosian, and Leonid dynasties
Under Khosrow II, the Sassanids occupied the Levant and  Egypt  and  advanced  into  Asia  Minor,  and  the Avars and Slavs raided in the Balkans. [73]   The Empire's  control  of  Italy  also  weakened. [74] After successfully  repelling  a  siege  of  Constantinople  in 626, [75] Heraclius won a decisive victory at the Battle of  Nineveh, [76] eventually  defeating  the  Sassanids later  that  year. [77] The  triumph  would  prove  shortlived. [78] The Arab conquests soon saw the conquest of the Levant, Egypt, and the Sassanid Empire by the newly formed Arab Rashidun Caliphate. [79]   By Heraclius' death in 641, the empire had been severely
reduced  economically  and  territorially-the  loss  of  the  wealthy  eastern  provinces  had  deprived  the empire of as much as three-quarters of its revenue. [80]
The next century is poorly documented. [81] Arab raids into Asia Minor started quickly, and the Empire responded by holding fortified centres and avoiding battle wherever possible. [82] Although Anatolia was invaded annually, it avoided permanent Arab occupation. [81] The outbreak of the First Fitna in 656 gave the  Empire  breathing  space,  which  it  used  sensibly: [83] some  order  was  restored  in  the  Balkans  by Constans II (r. 641-668) [84] following his administrative reorganisation which over time evolved into the "theme  system",  a  structure  that  allocated  troops  to  defend  specific  provinces. [85] Constantine  IV
(r. 668-685)  repelled  the  Arab  efforts  to  capture  Constantinople  in  the  670s  using  Greek  fire, [86] but suffered  a  reversal  against  the  Bulgars,  who  soon  established  an  empire  in  the  northern  Balkans. [87] Nevertheless,  he  had  done  enough  to  secure  the  empire's  position, [88] especially  as  the  Umayyad Caliphate was undergoing another civil war. [89]
Beginning in 695, when Constantine's son Justinian II was first deposed, the empire entered an era of political instability that lasted for the next 22 years. [90] While Justinian had stabilised the situation with the divided Arabs, [91] the threat of the reconstituted caliphate was met by Leo III when he repelled the 717-718 siege, the first serious challenge against Arab expansion. [92]
